content:
At six, I knew more or less how to dress appropriately for the weather. At twenty-six, I could not.

At six, I knew the rules: when it is cold, wear sweaters. When there is a lot of snow on the ground, wear parkas and snow pants and snow boots. When it is hot, wear t-shirts and shorts. I was happy to go outside every recess and play on the playground, or the grass, or the snow, because I followed the rules.

At twenty-six I had more than a decade's experience of breaking the rules, and I was less delicate: I could tolerate being a little cold or a little hot without throwing a tantrum. Dressing appropriately for the weather frequently trades off against aesthetics, and I had grown to be quite an aesthete.

If you are an aesthete about your wardrobe, here is what happens. Your good winter coat goes out of style, or you lose it at a party, and you don't bother to buy a new one because the fall jackets you have drape better anyways, so why not just suck it up and wear those. You wear through your old boots and get new ones almost purely for how cool they look, rather than evaluating them on their ability to keep you warm and dry through the Canadian winter.

At some point, I stopped seeing clothing as technology, and started seeing it as decoration. I have a summer wardrobe, thin fabrics that I can layer, and a winter wardrobe where I play with knits and wools and fur, and twice a year I switch out what's in the storage tub and what's in my closet. If you live in a city, you don't really need to think about it more than that.

Then, I was tricked by some friends into going winter camping in the Yukon.

Up in the far north, even in the bright sun of midday, as soon as I got out of the heated car I began to freeze. My toes lost sensation halfway through the short walk despite my socks and lined boots, my thin wool gloves absorbed the cold, attracted little ice crystals, and began to suck the heat from my fingertips. The cold found its way through every little crevice of my bulky sweater and my down parka to trail its fingers up my belly and down my neck.

The walk from the car to the building where we were to be kitted up with our rented deepwinter gear took three minutes, and it would take thirty for the feeling to half-return to my toes.

A few pieces of the appropriate winter gear were brand new to me — the Sorel Glaciers, for example, with their huge chunky rubber bottom soles, a thick removable inner boot, a third layer of insole inside the inner boot; all those separate layers to insulate you from the ground that you walk upon.

But most of what we rented turned out to be stuff you can buy at any sporting goods store — polyester (😔) quarter zips and thermal leggings. It was given to us along with the layering advice I had been hearing and ignoring since time immemorial: wear multiple layers, tuck them into each other so the cold air can't get in, cover up your skin with hats and scarves. We layered larger parkas over smaller puffer coats, thick mittens over gloves over an inner thin glove, three layers of bottoms and then waterproof snowpants on top.

Thus dressed, I went outside again. And then, for the first time since I was small, I felt free. I could go inspect the parked sleds that we would be learning to use, go play with the dogs in their enclosures, amble to the treeline and look up at the generously snow-laden branches.

When you are not dressed for the weather, being outside imposes a small, continual cost. You want to get out of the rain, the cold, the beating sun. That was okay though, you assure yourself, because it was only for a little bit of time, and you would soon be comfortable inside again.

I made a little bargain in this shape over and over again, aesthetics over function, until it became second nature, and the understanding that I could be comfortable outside if only I was dressed for it turned as abstract as the knowledge that the earth was round and not flat.

In the frozen northern -35°C windchill, I felt freer outside than I ever did in southern Ontario. I had an abundance of time; I didn't have to plan out the most efficient path. How queer, how sweet, how luxurious.

Now I have a rack of coats suitable for every degree of cold and wet, and a small new collection of pretty wool scarves. Without the nudge of the Yukon trip, left to my own devices, I would have accumulated a rack of fall jackets and weird pants. Now I buy a greater panoply of things, careful to make sure that they are not only beautiful but fill functional holes in my wardrobe.

In shitty weather I used to walk to the bus stop grim-faced and hunched over. These days, I dress well, and leave ten minutes early so I can loop by my favourite neighbourhood cafe for a little treat. In July I enjoy the crash of rain, in January the crunch of snow. I want to keep ambling, and I often do.
